meta.title: Who really said "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Mary Oliver — the closing lines of "The Summer Day" (House of Light, Beacon Press, 1990). Correctly credited, but almost always misquoted, and in copyright until 2090: fine to read aloud at a funeral, not free to put on merchandise.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing two lines of ‘The Summer Day,’ first collected in House of Light (Beacon Press, 1990). The attribution is almost never the problem with this one — the wording is. As published it reads “Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?”, with the ‘Tell me,’ intact and a line break after ‘plan to do.’

source.excerpt: Tell me, what else should I have done? Doesn't everything die at last, and too soon? Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?
trail: Beacon Press — Oliver’s original publisher — prints the poem with the credit line ‘Copyright © 1990 by Mary Oliver. First published in House of Light, Beacon Press,’ confirming poem, collection, publisher and year Beacon Broadside ↗.

The Academy of American Poets carries the licensed full text, reprinted by permission of the Charlotte Sheedy Literary Agency as agent for the author — which both fixes the canonical wording and shows the live permissions chain poets.org ↗.
The estate site states that NW Orchard LLC owns, by assignment, all intellectual property created by Mary Oliver, and routes permissions through the Sheedy agency maryoliver.com ↗.
Beacon’s own re-use policy is explicit: ‘Please do not distribute Mary Oliver’s poetry without permission’ — all uses require advance clearance re-use policy ↗.
source.excerptNote: The poem’s final four lines. The famous quotation is the last two — note the line break after ‘plan to do,’ which nearly every reproduction collapses.

source.rightsNote: In copyright until 1 January 2090. Published 1990; Mary Oliver died 17 January 2019, so the term runs life plus 70 years. Rights are held by NW Orchard LLC, and MARY OLIVER® is additionally a registered trademark — which matters for merchandise even beyond the text. Practical read: reading the two lines aloud in a eulogy or putting them on a memorial program with credit is the low-risk end, and a brief credited quotation on a lecture slide is a strong fair-use posture. Reproducing it in a book, a paid course, or on anything for sale needs written permission (Charlotte Sheedy Literary Agency). For poetry, ‘it’s only two lines’ is not a defence — two lines can be a substantial part of a short poem. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mary Oliver
author.heading: Mary Oliver
author.bio: Mary Oliver (1935–2019) won the Pulitzer Prize for American Primitive (1983) and the National Book Award for New and Selected Poems (1992). She wrote plainly and closely about the natural world — grasshoppers, ponds, geese, mornings — and turned that attention into questions about how a person ought to live. That combination made her one of the most quoted poets in America, and one of the most frequently misquoted: her lines travel far past her books, onto cards, headstones and slides, usually trimmed.

misattribution.heading: Right poet, wrong words
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a quote this famous, the attribution is almost always correct — people know it is Mary Oliver. What goes wrong is the text itself, and the assumption that a much-loved line is free to use.

items.why: The most common reproduction begins ‘What is it you plan to do…’, cutting the ‘Tell me,’ that makes it a direct address to the reader. Others rewrite it as ‘What will you do with your one wild and precious life?’ — changing the verb outright canonical text ↗.
Widely sold journals and prints drop the ‘and’ (‘one wild precious life’) or swap ‘your’ for ‘this.’ The line break after ‘plan to do’ is almost universally collapsed into prose.
Because the poem is beloved and widely reposted, people treat it as public domain. It is not, and will not be until 2090; the estate requires advance permission for reuse Beacon re-use policy ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Mary Oliver, ‘The Summer Day’ (1990) — quote it in full, with the line break, and clear permission before selling or publishing it licensed text ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The question lands so hard because of what comes before it. Most of the poem is Oliver doing nothing in particular — kneeling in the grass, watching a grasshopper eat sugar from her hand, admitting she does not know exactly what a prayer is. She earns the closing question by first paying close attention to something small.
Then she turns it on the reader: everything dies at last, and too soon, so — what do you plan to do? It works at funerals and graduations for the same reason, which is why it turns up at both.
detailsBody: As published: ‘Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?’
Most common variant: ‘What will you do with your one wild and precious life?’
Also seen: ‘What is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?’ (‘Tell me,’ dropped)
On merchandise: ‘your one wild precious life’ (‘and’ dropped) and ‘this one wild and precious life.’
